content.text: An HTTP 200 from the Claude API means your request was processed, not that the answer is complete. Every successful response carries a

that says why Claude stopped: it finished, hit your token cap, filled the context window, called a tool, paused, or refused. Read it on every call and handle each value, because several of them look like a normal answer until a user reads the end.

Your support dashboard shows an AI summary of each ticket. QA files a bug: some summaries stop mid-sentence, like "The customer was charged twice and asked for". The logs show HTTP 200 for every call, no exceptions, no retries. A week later, the summary worker crashes on one ticket with
IndexError: list index out of range
, again after a 200. Both bugs come from the same field nobody reads. The long tickets came back with
"If the Claude API returned a response without an error, the answer is complete." It's the rule most HTTP APIs teach:

items.text: In most APIs, a 200 means success and the body is the result you asked for.
The SDKs raise exceptions for failed requests, so no exception feels like no problem.
In development, prompts are short and almost every response ends naturally.
A truncated answer still reads like an answer, and a cut-off sentence is easy to miss in a log.

content.text: The half-truth: a 200 really does mean the request succeeded. But "the API processed your request" and "Claude gave you the whole answer you wanted" are two different facts, and the API reports the second one separately.
Errors and stop reasons answer different questions
Errors come back as HTTP 4xx or 5xx with error details, and they mean the request failed. The
is part of every successful response. In the docs' words, "Unlike errors, which indicate failures in processing your request,
tells you why Claude completed its response generation." In a non-streaming response it's never null, and the API reference lists seven values:

rows.text: Claude reached a natural stopping point
Output hit your cap or the model's context window
Don't treat it as complete: raise the cap, continue, or mark it
Claude called your tool, or a server-tool loop paused
Run the tool and send results, or send the response back
A safety classifier declined the request
, discard partial output, try a fallback

content.text: max_tokens is a ceiling, not a target
to generate before stopping", and the reference adds that models "may stop
reaching this maximum". When the answer needs more, generation stops at the cap, and the response is still a 200 with whatever text fit.
is the same situation one level up: the output filled the model's whole context window, and the docs' advice is to treat the response as truncated.
You have three honest options. Raise

so complete answers fit. Mark the output as truncated, as the docs' own example does with a note appended to the text. Or continue it: the docs show a loop that sends the original prompt, the partial text as an assistant turn and a user message asking Claude to continue, for a few attempts at most.
Two values mean the turn isn't over and Claude is waiting on your code. With
, Claude asked for one of your tools; you run it and send back a

, a server tool such as web search hit its iteration limit, 10 per request by default, and you send the response back as-is to let Claude finish. Saving either one as the final answer drops the actual work.
A refusal is a normal response
"Safety classifiers return this stop reason as a normal HTTP 200 response, not an error." On a refusal,
can be empty when the refusal arrives before any output, which is exactly what crashed

. A refusal can also arrive mid-stream after partial text; the docs say to "treat any partial output as incomplete and discard it". On current models, retrying the same request on another Claude model can usually serve it.
Here's the summary worker before and after it reads the field:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize:\n{ticket}"}],
)
# A 200 every time. Long tickets end mid-sentence ("max_tokens"), and a
# refusal with empty content raises IndexError on this line.
save_summary(reply.content[0].text)

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=4096,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize:\n{ticket}"}],
)
text = next((b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text"), "")
match reply.stop_reason:
    case "end_turn":
        save_summary(text)
    case "max_tokens" | "model_context_window_exceeded":
        log.warning("Summary truncated: %s", reply.stop_reason)
        save_summary(text + " [truncated]", complete=False)
    case "refusal":  # discard any partial text
        log.warning("Refused: %s", reply.stop_details)
        queue_for_fallback(ticket)
    case other:  # no tools or stop sequences here, so this is a bug
        raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected stop_reason: {other}")

content.text: The second version reads text by block type instead of assuming
, gives the summary room to finish, and turns each non-finished outcome into an explicit state. The last
matters too: if a future change adds tools to this call, a
response fails loudly instead of being saved as a summary.
deserves a glance. The docs note that Claude sometimes returns an empty response with
, typically right after tool results, and that resending the empty response unchanged won't help.

on one endpoint is an early warning that its inputs grew.
How to apply it in your project
Handle each value the call can produce, and make an unexpected value fail loudly instead of passing as success.
Set the cap from what complete answers actually need, and treat a truncated response as its own state in your data.
, discard partial output, and decide on a fallback model or a human path.
Count stop reasons per endpoint in your metrics, so truncation shows up on a dashboard before it shows up in a bug.

Branch on every value, fail loudly on unexpected ones, and track the mix in your metrics.
